transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-27 14:30 PST
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SRE), Alan Turner (Cobalt Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Cobalt Platform Eng), Rajiv Patel (Cobalt SecOps)
Links shared: benchmark sheet (trimmed): https://redwood.app/benchmarks/cobalt-prefetch-2026 , security pack: https://redwood.app/security/cobalt

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on throughput tuning for Cobalt's inference surface. Focus areas: prefetch/prefill profiles for KV cache, scheduler knobs including fair-queueing and burst smoothing, choosing max_num_seqs vs token-limits, and quantization tradeoffs (int8/int4). Also discussed VPC/on-prem constraints and prewarm strategies to reduce cold-cache tail.

Topics: prefetch profiles, max_num_seqs, token caps, continuous batching behavior, KV cache cold-start, quantization impact on throughput, VPC networking egress and warmup, rollback/fallback policies.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to focus on the throughput tuning items you highlighted in the intake doc, specifically those prefetch and scheduler questions. Are we good to run with that agenda?
[00:12] Alan (Cobalt): Yep that works. We have a couple of p99 SLAs that are slipping under peaky loads, and the cost is spiking when we try to blunt the tail.
[00:20] Liam (Redwood SE): Cool, can you give a super short picture of your workload? average seq len, batchiness, any long context users?
[00:30] Sofia (Cobalt): Mostly chat-ish, average user prompt+history ~220 tokens, responses ~120 tokens. But we have spikes when a single workflow runs multi-step generation and that pushes seq length to 1k sometimes. RPS baseline 45, bursts to 600 for 10-20s windows.
[00:50] Priya (Redwood SRE): and are these bursts multi-tenant? i.e the same customer id or cross-tenant?
[00:55] Sofia: Mixed. 70% normal cross-tenant, 30% from internal automated flows that are a single tenant - those are the ones that thrash the kv cache.
[01:05] Liam: ok that explains the cold KV-hit tail. two levers that help: prefetch profiles (warm kv for common prefixes) and max_num_seqs tuning so schedulers don't pack too many long seqs together and cause OOM or long stalls.
[01:25] Alan: Can you unpack prefetch profile? are we talking prefill or proactive KV prefetch?
[01:30] Liam: both terms get used. In Redwood we have a prefetch profile that will prime the KV cache with commonly-accessed KV entries for a model variant when a request matches a profile; think of it as a warmup trace we replay. It's heuristic-driven: prefix frequency, recent hit-rate, and payload histogram feed into the policy.
[01:48] Alan: Sounds great. How invasive is that on latency for cold requests?
[01:52] Liam: Minimal if tuned. There are short-path fast prefetches that run inline and cheaper background prefetches for larger warmups. The trick is choosing warmup depth: prefetching too many cache pages hurts first-request latency; too few leaves tail up.
[02:08] Rajiv (Cobalt): any security concerns? can prefetch read tenant data into shared caches in a way that violates isolation?
[02:14] Maya: good callout. For Dedicated/VPC we honor tenant isolation; prefetch only primes model-specific KV entries and respects tenant sharding. For hosted multi-tenant we avoid cross-tenant warming unless you opt-in and we provide an isolated pre-warm lane. We'll follow up with the security notes in the pack.
[02:34] Sofia: ok next, max_num_seqs, we saw a recommended 64 in your docs. but our seqs vary widely, 64 seems blunt.
[02:44] Liam: yes 64 is a common default but not a golden rule. There are two dimensions: max_num_seqs and token ceilings (token per batch). If you only cap max_num_seqs you can still end up with many short sequences that are cheap, but a single long seq can hog the window. We often recommend a composite guard: max_num_seqs = 48 with token cap = 12000 tokens per batch for your profile.
[03:10] Alan: how do we pick token caps?
[03:12] Liam: instrument: look at your payload histogram. For you with avg 340 tokens per request, and bursts of 600 RPS, a token cap around 12k keeps latency low while letting batching amortize kernel overhead. We ran a sim on your sample traces and the sheet shows the 12k point as the knee.
[03:29] Maya: linking the sim: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/cobalt-prefetch-2026 (see tab "token-knee")
[03:36] Sofia: i see the sheet, there's a column for cold-kv penalty. that seems to dominate at low warm hit rates.
[03:42] Liam: exactly. cold cache penalty can be 1.6-2x p99 depending on context-length. That's why we push for prefetching hot prefixes and prefix-based caching retention. Also adaptive eviction: keep hot prefixes pinned during known burst windows (we can hook to your traffic schedule).
[04:05] Alan: what's the scheduler knob surface? names etc so I can map to our config management.
[04:10] Liam: main knobs: max_num_seqs, token_cap_per_window, slot_size (controls GPU slice granularity), continuous_batching_enabled (bool), prefetch_profile (name/id), backpressure_threshold (queue depth at which we start shedding or degrade to smaller model), and priority_weights (for fair-queueing per-customer).
[04:30] Priya: slot_size? i thought that's internal. how does tweaking that help?
[04:34] Liam: slot_size affects how we pack sequences into GPU compute slices; larger slots mean fewer kernels and lower per-token overhead but higher latency for short tail. For your mix, a medium slot_size gave better throughput with acceptable p95. We can share the exact config snippet.
[04:50] Rajiv: about fair-queueing and tenant fairness — how do we prevent a noisy neighbor with large seqs from starving the rest?
[04:58] Liam: two approaches: reservation windows per-tenant or soft priority weights. We prefer soft weights + drain cycles: the scheduler enforces a max continuous window per tenant (e.g., 200ms) and then rotates. Combined with token ceilings prevents single tenant dominance.
[05:15] Alan: in practice how do we set weights for internal vs external traffic?
[05:18] Maya: typical pattern: internal automated flows get a lower weight but higher reservation during known batch windows; external prod traffic gets higher baseline weight. We can show a starter mapping.
[05:28] Sofia: can we do canary changes? I'm nervous about changing token caps in prod.
[05:32] Liam: yes, Redwood supports staged rollout: canary on 5% traffic, monitor p50/p95/p99 token-hitrate, and auto rollback if p99 increases by more than x%. We also support synthetic replay for your sample trace to validate before rollout.
[05:46] Alan: you mentioned quantization earlier — will INT4 help throughput for us? we run an LLaMA derivative.
[05:52] Liam: quanization (sic) helps, but tradeoffs: int8 is safer for quality in many models; int4 gives 1.6-1.9x token throughput gains on compatible kernels but may regress output quality for some instruction-following tasks. For your template generation we saw small nq drops with int4 unless we apply per-layer scaling and a tiny re-calibration. We can run a quick A/B on a representative eval set.
[06:16] Priya: are the int4 kernels available in VPC/private?
[06:19] Liam: yes, same runtime codepath but kernel perf depends on GPU and driver. We'll run a node-level microbenchmark in your on-prem match if you want.
[06:27] Rajiv: about VPC networking — our security team worries about cold-starts causing egress spikes to S3 during model load/warm.
[06:34] Maya: good note. Our private deployment supports local model caching and optional preloaded snapshots to avoid heavy S3 pulls. For hosted we do staged pulls and prefetch parallelism throttles to avoid egress storms. We'll include recommended AWS/GCS prewarm configs in the security pack.
[06:50] Sofia: what about metrics to watch during tuning?
[06:53] Liam: token per second, batch sizes, kv_hit_rate, kernel_utilization (GPU SM%), evictions/sec, and request age (time since first token). Also track cost per 1k tokens for different configs. Our console exposes these per model and per route.
[07:10] Alan: is there an automated optimizer? you mentioned Redwood Optimize earlier.
[07:14] Liam: yes, Optimize can suggest a profile — it will run short experiments in a staging pool and recommend max_num_seqs, token caps, and prefetch depth. For your workload it suggested the 48/12k profile with aggressive prefetch for top-20 prefixes. We still encourage manual review before rollout.
[07:31] Sophia (Customer): Sorry I missed a name — is Optimize a paid add-on?
[07:34] Maya: Optimize is an add-on; we can include a trial during pilot.
[07:38] Rajiv: circling back to rollback/fallback — can we route to a smaller model if kernel latency spikes?
[07:44] Liam: yes, smart routing policies let you fallback to a smaller quantized variant or a lower context model. Redwood can do automatic fallback when queue depth or kernel lat exceeds thresholds. You define the policy.
[07:56] Alan: show me results from your sim about p99 under bursts again?
[07:59] Liam: (screen share) here: baseline no-prefetch, default 64: p99 ~ 1.9s during a 600 RPS 15s burst. With prefetch profile and 48/12k caps p99 drops to 1.1s and cost per token drops ~22%. If we add int8 quant and moderate slot sizing, p99 0.95s and cost down ~30%. Int4 gets cost down more but we flagged quality delta for two prompt types.
[08:30] Sofia: that's promising. What's the effort to pilot? and timeline?
[08:34] Maya: pilot plan: 1) dry-run using your traces on Redwood staging (we'll need sample traces) 2) canary with 5% traffic and monitoring for 48-72 hours 3) expand to 25% then 100% if metrics stable. Typical pilot 2-4 weeks end-to-end.
[08:50] Alan: security sign-off path? Rajiv?
[08:53] Rajiv: we'll need SOC2 controls, KMS integration, and a list of network ports plus model residency guarantees. Also proof that prefetch won't leak tenant data into shared caches.
[09:03] Maya: we'll send the security pack with the prefetch isolation doc; we can set up a call with Redwood security if needed.
[09:10] Liam: note: prefetch isolation for multi-tenant means we only materialize tenant-specific KV when tenant isolation is enabled; for hosted multi-tenant we default to namespace isolation, and for Dedicated/VPC it's physical isolation. We'll attach the technical note.
[09:26] Sofia: one final question: how do we measure p99 regressions from quantization?
[09:30] Liam: you run inference evals (ROUGE/ROBT A? transcrip-ble) on a holdout prompt set. We provide diff tools to compare embeddings/semantics and a human spot-check for instruction behavior. Our eval harness outputs quality deltas and flags prompts with regressions.
[09:48] Alan: ok let's wrap up with concrete next steps.
[09:51] Maya: recap: Redwood sends trimmed benchmarks + cost calc + prefetch profile examples; Liam sends scheduler config snippets and sample canary policy; Cobalt provides production traces, payload histogram, and security checklist. We aim to kick the pilot week of 2026-12-07.
[10:06] Rajiv: i'll confirm the security checklist items and get the SecOps folks on the pilot call.
[10:12] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via the shared board with the artifacts and next meeting invite.

End transcript
